title: Iqbal's address to the Muslim League, 1930
body: In 1930, Sir Muhammad Iqbal, as president of the Muslim League, spoke about the place of Muslims in a free India. He said that if the Indian Muslim was recognised as entitled to full and free development on the lines of his own culture and tradition, he would be ready to stake his all for the freedom of India. He argued that the units of Indian society were not territorial, as in European countries, and that European democracy could not be applied to India without recognising communal groups. He noted that many Hindus thought separate electorates were contrary to true nationalism, because they understood a nation as a universal amalgamation in which no community kept its own identity. Iqbal replied that India was a land of racial and religious variety, and he pointed to the economic inferiority of Muslims, their heavy debt, especially in Punjab, and their insufficient majorities in some provinces. This, he said, explained the anxiety of Muslims to retain separate electorates.
